title: The seven churches of Rome
hook: Philip Neri's walking pilgrimage with picnics and songs

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Camino de Santiago: yellow arrows, scallop shells, and strangers wishing each other a good road. Your line was buen camino. Who did you wish well on their way? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

Early morning in Rome, centuries ago. A crowd gathers around a priest who is known for jokes as much as for prayer. Shopkeepers, students, a few nobles, some boys from the streets. They set off on foot together, singing. They stop at one great church, pray, and walk on to the next. Somewhere in the middle of the day, they sit down in a garden and eat lunch together: bread, wine, cheese, fruit. Then musicians play, and the crowd walks on to the next church, and the next, until evening. The priest is Philip Neri. And this walking, praying, singing, picnicking day has a name. Today, the seven churches.
screen: `A CROWD SETS OFF, SINGING.` → `PRAYER, THEN THE NEXT CHURCH.` → `LUNCH IN A GARDEN.`

segments.voice: The visit to the seven churches is an old Roman pilgrimage: a long walk in one day to seven of the city's great churches. Saint Peter's. Saint Paul Outside the Walls. Saint John Lateran. Saint Mary Major. Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls. Holy Cross in Jerusalem. Saint Sebastian, by the catacombs. Pilgrims had made this round before Philip. Tradition says he turned it into something crowds could join. First, who Philip was. A priest in Rome, remembered as the saint of joy. Stories about him are full of jokes, odd hats and teasing, which, the stories say, kept him, and others, from taking themselves too seriously. Second, why a walk. Tradition says Philip led these walks partly as a cheerful alternative to the rowdiness of carnival season. Instead of telling people what not to do, he gave them a better day out. Third, why the picnic. This is the surprising part. A pilgrimage could have been grim and silent. Philip made eating together part of it. Sitting on the grass with strangers became part of the prayer, not a break from it. The Psalms put it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity." Good, and pleasant. Both words. Last, the walk itself is still made. Parishes and groups in Rome keep the custom, and pilgrims still trace the route on foot. The churches are far apart. The feet get tired. The lunch still tastes good.
screen: `SEVEN GREAT CHURCHES, ONE DAY.` · `PHILIP, THE SAINT OF JOY.` · `A BETTER DAY OUT THAN CARNIVAL.` · `THE PICNIC IS PART OF THE PRAYER.` · then, large: `HOW GOOD AND HOW PLEASANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a visit to two churches in one day. Two, not seven. Settle, and breathe. Think of two churches you could reach in a single afternoon. They don't have to be grand. Picture walking into the first and sitting for a minute. Then picture the stretch between them, and where you could stop to eat. A bench, a café, a park. Who could come with you? Philip walked in a crowd. If you pray, you can say one Our Father in each church. If you don't, just sit in each for a minute and notice what's different. The bell holds the time.
The seven churches of Rome. A one-day walking pilgrimage to seven great churches, which Philip Neri made joyful with songs and a shared lunch. Today's word.
screen: `THE SEVEN CHURCHES OF ROME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: pilgrims with a picnic. Today, visit two churches, or plan when you will, and share some food with someone along the way. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

fork.setup: you're Philip Neri. carnival season is coming, and the young people of Rome are heading for the rowdy streets. what do you do?
options: preach a hard sermon against carnival.
lead them on a long walk to the churches, with music and lunch.
stay home and pray for them.
fork.reveal: tradition says he gave them a better day out: a walking pilgrimage with songs and a picnic in a garden.

trapdoor: what you thought: a tour of Rome's famous churches.
what it means: a one-day walking pilgrimage to seven churches, which Philip Neri made joyful, with singing and a shared meal.
what a scholar hears: Philip didn't start the round; tradition credits him with turning it into a popular, cheerful pilgrimage, partly as an alternative to carnival.

sources.quoted: Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.

notes: No dates given for Philip Neri or the walk. The list of the seven churches (with Saint Sebastian rather than the Sanctuary of Divine Love, which some modern itineraries substitute): confirm.

Claims that pilgrims made the round before Philip, that tradition credits him with making it popular partly as an alternative to carnival, and the garden lunch with music: drawn from traditional lives of Philip. Confirm.
'Remembered as the saint of joy' and the stories of jokes and odd hats: traditional; confirm the framing.
'Parishes and groups in Rome keep the custom': confirm it is still made.

Editor: 'something a whole city could join' softened to 'tradition says he turned it into something crowds could join'; the garbled 'teasing, played to keep himself' sentence rewritten; 'Philip never walked alone' (an absolute) became 'Philip walked in a crowd'.
